The numbers 1, 2, ..., 2100 are written on a board. Every second, Mark takes two numbers on the board, \( a \) and \( b \), erases them, and replaces them with \( \gcd(a, b) \) and \( \operatorname{lcm}(a, b) \). Mark stops once any move he makes will not change the numbers written on the board. Compute the number of divisors of the 2026th smallest positive integer written on the board when he finishes.

Put your final answer within \boxed{}.

message.content:
Let \(N=2100\). We view the board as a multiset of \(N\) entries.

For a prime \(p\) and \(t\ge 1\), the number of board entries divisible by \(p^t\) is invariant under the move: for the two chosen numbers, their \(p\)-adic valuations are replaced by their minimum and maximum, so the number of those two with valuation at least \(t\) is unchanged. Initially this number is

\[
\left\lfloor \frac{2100}{p^t}\right\rfloor.
\]

A move changes the board exactly when the two chosen numbers are incomparable under divisibility. Thus when Mark finishes, the board is a divisibility chain. Since the 2026th smallest entry among \(2100\) entries is the \(2100-2026+1=75\)th largest entry, we only need to know which prime powers divide the 75th largest entry.

In a divisibility chain, the entries divisible by a fixed \(p^t\) form a suffix. Therefore the 75th largest entry is divisible by \(p^t\) iff at least \(75\) final entries are divisible by \(p^t\), i.e. iff

\[
\left\lfloor \frac{2100}{p^t}\right\rfloor \ge 75.
\]

So the exponent of \(p\) in the desired number is the largest \(t\) such that

\[
\left\lfloor \frac{2100}{p^t}\right\rfloor \ge 75.
\]

Now compute:

\[
\begin{array}{c|c}
p & \text{largest }t\text{ with }\left\lfloor 2100/p^t\right\rfloor\ge 75\\
\hline
2 & 4 \quad (\lfloor 2100/16\rfloor=131,\ \lfloor 2100/32\rfloor=65)\\
3 & 3 \quad (\lfloor 2100/27\rfloor=77,\ \lfloor 2100/81\rfloor=25)\\
5 & 2 \quad (\lfloor 2100/25\rfloor=84,\ \lfloor 2100/125\rfloor=16)\\
7,11,13,17,19,23 & 1\\
\end{array}
\]

No prime \(p\ge 29\) can occur, since \(\lfloor 2100/29\rfloor=72<75\).

Thus the 2026th smallest final number is

\[
2^4\cdot 3^3\cdot 5^2\cdot 7\cdot 11\cdot 13\cdot 17\cdot 19\cdot 23.
\]

Its number of positive divisors is

\[
(4+1)(3+1)(2+1)(1+1)^6
=5\cdot4\cdot3\cdot 2^6
=3840.
\]

\[
\boxed{3840}
\]
